title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
subject: Science
chapter: 13. Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
description: Why Earth alone sustains life — its position, size, atmosphere and magnetic field, the interacting Earth systems, reproduction and the threats of the triple planetary crisis.

questions.question: The image at the start of the chapter, taken by an ISRO Earth Observation Satellite, was built by combining roughly how many smaller images?
options: Nearly 3000 images
Nearly 300 images
Nearly 30 images
Nearly 30,000 images
questions.explanation: The chapter says the satellite picture was made by combining nearly 3000 smaller images, like pieces of a mosaic.

questions.question: Why is the ISRO satellite picture of Earth described as a 'false colour' image?
options: The camera could not record colours, so they were painted on afterwards
Colours stand for different kinds of information, not true appearance
Clouds hid the surface, so the colours were guessed from printed maps
It was taken at night, so the colours were added later by a computer
questions.explanation: In a false colour image scientists deliberately use different colours to show different types of information (e.g. plants, ocean temperature); it is not how Earth would look to the eye.

questions.question: Select the things the chapter says satellite images can help detect.
options: Oil spills
Age of rocks deep underground
Wind direction
Depth of the Earth's inner core
questions.explanation: Satellite images can detect ocean temperature, oil spills and wind direction, and help study plants on land and tiny organisms in the ocean. They do not reveal the age of deep rocks or the depth of the core.

questions.question: Which TWO of these does the chapter list among the things Earth provides us?
options: The air we breathe
The soil that helps grow crops
The light from distant stars
The heat from its inner core
questions.explanation: The chapter says Earth gives us the air we breathe, the water we drink, the soil for growing crops, and materials like rock and timber for building.

questions.question: If the Earth were the size of an apple, the crust would be as thin as which part of the apple?
options: the apple's core
half of the apple
the apple's skin
the apple's stalk
questions.explanation: Fig. 13.1 compares the crust to the thin skin of an apple — the layer where all life exists is tiny compared with the whole planet.

questions.question: From the tallest mountain to the deepest ocean trench, all known life on Earth is found in which layer?
options: The upper mantle
The outer core
The lower mantle
The crust
questions.explanation: All mountains, rivers, forests, animals and people are found on the crust — a very thin layer on the planet's surface.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the Earth's layers correctly from the surface inwards (Fig. 13.1)?
options: Crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core, inner core
Crust, outer core, upper mantle, lower mantle, inner core
Crust, lower mantle, upper mantle, inner core, outer core
Upper mantle, crust, lower mantle, outer core, inner core
questions.explanation: Fig. 13.1 labels, from outside in: crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core, inner core. The crust is outermost and the inner core is at the centre.

questions.question: Table 13.1 notes that the air we breathe stays around the Earth even though gas particles move freely and gases have no fixed volume.
questions.explanation: This is the first 'taken for granted' feature in Table 13.1 — Earth's gravity keeps the atmosphere from flying off into space even though gases spread freely.

questions.question: Life on Earth is spread through the whole planet, from the crust right down to the core.
questions.explanation: All life exists only in a very thin surface layer — the crust. Compared with the size of the Earth this layer is as thin as an apple's skin.

questions.question: Table 13.1 pairs 'we can stand on the ground held by gravity' with which surprising everyday fact?
options: Our bones never break under our own body weight
Our heart can still pump blood up to our head
The ground never sinks under very heavy buildings
Objects we drop always fall at exactly the same speed
questions.explanation: The table points out that although gravity holds us down (Chapter 5), our heart manages to pump blood upwards to the head — an interesting feature we take for granted.

questions.question: Which materials does the chapter say the Earth provides for building homes, buildings and roads?
options: Coal and oil
Salt and iron
Rock and timber
Sand and glass
questions.explanation: The text says the Earth provides materials like rock and timber with which we build our homes, buildings and roads.

questions.question: Which statement about the Earth's crust is NOT correct?
options: It is where all known life exists
It is tiny compared to Earth's size
It is compared to the thin skin of an apple
It makes up most of the Earth's volume
questions.explanation: The crust is a very thin outer layer, tiny compared with the whole Earth — it does NOT make up most of the planet's volume. The other three statements come straight from the chapter.

questions.question: How many planets go around the Sun in our solar system?
options: Eight
Seven
Nine
Ten
questions.explanation: Our solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

questions.question: Which planet is the fourth from the Sun?
options: Venus
Mars
Jupiter
Earth
questions.explanation: In order of increasing distance from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — so Mars is fourth.

questions.question: Which group contains ONLY the small, rocky planets?
options: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, Mars
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
Earth, Mars, Saturn, Neptune
questions.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are relatively small and rocky; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are large planets mostly made of gases.

questions.question: In Table 13.2 the eighth planet has an average temperature of about −200 °C and a radius 4 times Earth's. Which planet is it?
options: Uranus
Saturn
Jupiter
Neptune
questions.explanation: Row 8 of Table 13.2 is the planet farthest from the Sun — Neptune — with −200 °C and radius 4 (compared to Earth = 1).

questions.question: Table 13.2 gives the fifth planet from the Sun a radius about 11 times that of Earth. Which planet is this?
options: Jupiter
Saturn
Uranus
Neptune
questions.explanation: The fifth planet from the Sun is Jupiter, the largest planet, with a radius about 11 times Earth's.

questions.question: According to Table 13.2, which planet has NO atmosphere?
options: Venus
Mercury
Neptune
Earth
questions.explanation: Table 13.2 marks Mercury as having no atmosphere; the text later confirms 'Mercury has no atmosphere at all'.

questions.question: How does the chapter describe the shape of the planets' orbits around the Sun?
options: highly elongated ovals
perfectly square paths
nearly circular
spiral paths inward
questions.explanation: The eight planets go around the Sun in nearly circular orbits. This keeps the sunlight a planet receives fairly steady through the year.

questions.question: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are large planets mostly made of gases.
questions.explanation: The chapter divides the planets into four small rocky ones (Mercury to Mars) and four large, mostly gaseous ones (Jupiter to Neptune).

questions.question: Mercury, being closest to the Sun, has the highest average temperature of all the planets.
questions.explanation: Venus (450 °C) is hotter than Mercury (170 °C). Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat through the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: Table 13.2 gives Venus's radius as 0.95 compared to Earth's 1. What does this tell you?
options: Venus is slightly larger than Earth
Venus is less than half Earth's size
Venus is almost twice Earth's size
Venus is slightly smaller than Earth
questions.explanation: The radius column compares each planet to Earth (= 1). A value of 0.95 means Venus is only a little smaller than Earth.

questions.question: A planet lies farther from the Sun than Earth. Based on the general trend in Table 13.2, what would you expect?
options: It is colder than Earth on average
It is hotter than Earth on average
It has the same temperature as Earth
It must have a thicker atmosphere
questions.explanation: Planets get their energy from the Sun, so moving farther from the Sun generally makes a planet colder (Venus is the exception, because of its atmosphere).

questions.question: Select the TWO planets that are small and rocky.
options: Mars
Saturn
Venus
Uranus
questions.explanation: Mars and Venus belong to the rocky group (with Mercury and Earth). Saturn and Uranus are large gas planets.

questions.question: Mercury averages 170 °C while Venus averages 450 °C. Which statement explains this correctly?
options: Venus is closer to the Sun than Mercury, so it receives more energy
Venus's thick CO2 atmosphere traps heat; Mercury has none to trap it
Mercury's rocky surface reflects all the sunlight back into space
Venus is larger, and bigger planets always hold on to more heat
questions.explanation: Venus is the hottest planet not because it is closest (Mercury is) but because its thick, almost entirely CO2 atmosphere traps heat. Mercury has no atmosphere at all.

questions.question: The air on Venus is almost entirely made up of which gas?
options: Water vapour
Nitrogen gas
Carbon dioxide
Methane gas
questions.explanation: The air on Venus is almost entirely carbon dioxide, which does not let heat escape — causing a very strong greenhouse effect.

questions.question: On Earth, how do gases like carbon dioxide trap heat?
options: By reflecting sunlight before it reaches the ground
By blocking ultraviolet rays like the ozone layer does
By holding warm air in place as a closed glass room does
By absorbing radiation given off by the warmed Earth
questions.explanation: After the Sun warms the Earth, the Earth gives off radiation; greenhouse gases absorb this radiation so the heat does not escape.

questions.question: How does a greenhouse for growing plants differ from the greenhouse effect on Venus or Earth?
options: It traps warmed air because it is a closed space
It traps heat by gases absorbing Earth's radiation
It cools the air inside by blocking all the sunlight
It works only at night when the ground radiates
questions.explanation: A plant greenhouse is a closed space, usually with glass walls, so warmed air cannot leave. On a planet, gases absorb radiation — both keep things warm but in different ways.

questions.question: The greenhouse effect plays an important role in maintaining the right temperature on Earth.
questions.explanation: Though mild, Earth's greenhouse effect keeps the temperature just high enough for water to stay liquid.

questions.question: A plant greenhouse and Venus's atmosphere warm things in exactly the same way.
questions.explanation: They work differently: a plant greenhouse simply traps warmed air in a closed glass space, while Venus's CO2 absorbs radiation given off by the warmed surface.

questions.question: If Earth had no atmosphere, what does the chapter say would happen to its heat?
options: It would build up and Earth would become far too hot
It would be lost to space and Earth would become too cold
It would stay the same because the Sun still shines on it
It would move into the core and heat the mantle instead
questions.explanation: Without an atmosphere the Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold. The greenhouse effect helps keep the Earth warm.

questions.question: Which statement about the greenhouse effect is NOT correct?
options: It makes Venus even hotter than Mercury is
It keeps Earth warm enough for liquid water to exist
It is caused mainly by oxygen in the atmosphere
It is produced by gases like carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases are gases like carbon dioxide (and methane), not oxygen. The other statements are correct according to the chapter.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of events in Earth's greenhouse effect?
options: CO2 absorbs sunlight; Earth warms; Earth radiates; heat escapes
Earth radiates; Sun warms Earth; CO2 reflects heat; heat is kept
Sun warms CO2; CO2 warms Earth; Earth radiates; heat escapes
Sun warms Earth; Earth radiates; CO2 absorbs radiation; heat is kept
questions.explanation: The Sun warms the Earth first; the warmed Earth gives off radiation; carbon dioxide absorbs that radiation; so the heat is retained rather than escaping.

questions.question: Which TWO are needed for the greenhouse effect shown in Fig. 13.2 on Earth?
options: Radiation given off by the warmed Earth
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
Glass walls surrounding the planet
Molten iron moving in the core
questions.explanation: Earth's greenhouse effect needs the Earth to radiate heat after being warmed by the Sun, and greenhouse gases such as CO2 to absorb it. Glass walls belong to a plant greenhouse; molten iron relates to the magnetic field.

questions.question: What is the name for the trapping of heat by gases in a planet's atmosphere?
options: Greenhouse effect
Habitable zone
Ozone layer effect
Geodiversity
questions.explanation: The trapping of heat by atmospheric gases such as carbon dioxide is called the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what is the MOST important reason the Earth can support life?
options: Its magnetic field
Its distance from the Sun
Its nearly circular orbit
Its large size and gravity
questions.explanation: The most important reason is Earth's distance from the Sun — just right for the temperature to allow liquid water.

questions.question: If the Earth were much closer to the Sun, what would happen to its water?
options: all water would freeze
water would stay liquid
all water would evaporate
oceans would get deeper
questions.explanation: Closer to the Sun it would be too hot and all the water would evaporate; farther away it would be too cold and all the water would freeze.

questions.question: If the Earth were much farther from the Sun, the chapter says that:
options: all the water would evaporate
water would become salty
water would stay liquid
all the water would freeze
questions.explanation: Too far from the Sun it would be too cold and all the water would freeze, making life as we know it impossible.

questions.question: The habitable zone around a star is also known as the:
options: Goldilocks zone
Greenhouse zone
Blue zone
Solar zone
questions.explanation: The range of distances where water remains liquid is called the habitable zone, or sometimes the 'Goldilocks zone' — not too hot, not too cold, just right.

questions.question: Which is the correct description of a star's habitable zone?
options: Range of distances where a planet has a magnetic field
Range of distances from a star where water stays liquid
Region of a planet's crust where life is actually found
Zone of a planet's atmosphere that contains the ozone layer
questions.explanation: The habitable zone is the range of distances from the Sun (or another star) over which water remains in liquid form.

questions.question: According to the chapter, no life form at all can survive in frozen environments.
questions.explanation: The chapter says some microbes, like certain bacteria, can survive in frozen environments — but liquid water is still essential for life to evolve.

questions.question: Why is the Earth called the Blue Planet?
options: Its atmosphere is mostly blue nitrogen
Its oceans reflect the blue magnetic field
Most of its surface is covered with water
Its sky appears blue when seen from space
questions.explanation: Seen from space, Earth looks blue because of the vast amount of water covering most of its surface — hence 'Blue Planet'.

questions.question: Where does Mars lie in relation to the Sun's habitable zone?
options: At the centre of the habitable zone
Far outside the habitable zone
Closer to the Sun than the zone
At the edge of the habitable zone
questions.explanation: Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone, which is one reason it might once have had liquid water.

questions.question: What have the spacecraft and rovers sent to Mars found so far regarding life?
options: No proof of life so far
Fossils of simple plants
Living bacteria in lakes
Clear signs of flowing rivers today
questions.explanation: Rovers have explored the surface, but no proof of life has been found yet. Scientists only think Mars MAY have had liquid water in the past.

questions.question: Why does Mars continue to interest scientists?
options: It currently has oceans like Earth's
It may once have had liquid water and lakes
It has a thicker atmosphere than Earth
It has a stronger magnetic field than Earth
questions.explanation: Scientists think Mars may have had liquid water — maybe even lakes — and conditions for simple life in the past. Its atmosphere today is 100 times thinner than Earth's.

questions.question: The chapter says science stays open to change when we learn more.
questions.explanation: Using Mars as an example, the chapter notes that science doesn't always have final answers and stays open to change as new clues are found.

questions.question: What is one major reason Mars cannot currently support life like Earth?
options: It has far too many erupting volcanoes
It orbits much too close to the Sun
It lacks a thick atmosphere and liquid water
Its magnetic field is far too strong
questions.explanation: Mars's atmosphere is 100 times thinner than Earth's and it has no liquid water today. It is at the edge of the habitable zone, not too close to the Sun.

questions.question: Earth's distance from the Sun allows water to remain mostly in liquid form.
questions.explanation: Being at the right distance keeps temperatures in the range where water stays liquid — essential for the development and sustenance of life.

questions.question: What is the effect of Earth's nearly circular orbit on life?
options: Days and nights are of equal length all year round
The Earth never gets any closer to the Sun at all
The magnetic field keeps pointing the same way
Sunlight and heat stay nearly steady through the year
questions.explanation: A nearly circular orbit keeps the amount of sunlight and heat nearly steady throughout the year, preventing extreme summers and winters at most places.

questions.question: If the Earth were smaller but had the same density, what might happen to its atmosphere?
options: It would escape into space due to weaker gravity
It would become much thicker and hotter
It would freeze solid onto the surface
It would cause far stronger winds to blow
questions.explanation: A smaller Earth would have weaker gravity, too weak to hold on to the gases of the atmosphere, which would escape into space — as happened on Mars and Mercury.

questions.question: How does the atmosphere of Mars compare with Earth's?
options: About 10 times thinner
About 100 times thinner
About the same thickness
About 100 times thicker
questions.explanation: On Mars the atmosphere is 100 times thinner than on Earth, and Mercury has no atmosphere at all.

questions.question: If the Earth were much larger with much stronger gravity, the chapter suggests that:
options: its atmosphere would escape
its water would all evaporate
gravity could crush our bones
the orbit would become oval
questions.explanation: A very large planet would pull us down with such force that our bones could be crushed. Escaping atmosphere is the problem of a planet that is too SMALL.

questions.question: An ozone molecule is made of how many oxygen atoms?
options: Two oxygen atoms
One oxygen atom
Four oxygen atoms
Three oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: Ozone is a three-atom oxygen molecule formed from some of the oxygen in the atmosphere.

questions.question: What is the main protective role of the ozone layer?
options: Blocks harmful UV rays from the Sun
Traps heat like a greenhouse gas
Pushes away cosmic rays and solar wind
Supplies oxygen for us to breathe
questions.explanation: The ozone layer acts like a shield, blocking harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays that can damage living cells. Deflecting charged particles is the magnetic field's job.

questions.question: The ozone layer protects the Earth by deflecting high-energy particles coming from the Sun.
questions.explanation: The ozone layer blocks ultraviolet rays. It is the Earth's magnetic field that pushes away high-energy particles such as the solar wind.

questions.question: In which year was India's Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission) launched?
questions.explanation: Mangalyaan was launched in 2013 by ISRO and showed that India could do space science with smart, low-cost technology.

questions.question: Mangalyaan carried tools to study which features of Mars?
options: the two moons of Mars and their many craters
the planet's rings and its magnetic poles
the atmosphere, surface and signs of past water
living organisms hidden in Martian soil
questions.explanation: The orbiter carried tools to study Mars's atmosphere, surface and signs of past water — helping ask whether Mars was ever suitable for life.

questions.question: Which statement about Mangalyaan is NOT correct?
options: It was launched by ISRO in 2013
It is also called the Mars Orbiter Mission
It used smart, low-cost technology
It landed a rover on the Martian surface
questions.explanation: Mangalyaan was an ORBITER — it studied Mars from orbit and did not land a rover. The other three statements match the chapter.

questions.question: Oxygen in the atmosphere is needed by almost all forms of life on Earth.
questions.explanation: The presence of oxygen allows us to breathe and is needed by almost all life forms; some oxygen also forms the protective ozone layer.

questions.question: Select the TWO conditions the chapter links to the Earth being the 'right size'.
options: Gravity strong enough to hold on to the atmosphere
Gravity weak enough not to crush living beings
A perfectly circular orbit around the Sun
A thick layer of carbon dioxide like Venus
questions.explanation: Earth's size gives gravity that is just enough to keep the atmosphere from escaping, yet not so strong that creatures would be crushed by their own weight.

questions.question: If there were no atmosphere on the Earth, which of these would follow?
options: Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold
The Earth's gravity would become much weaker
The Earth's orbit would become more elongated
The Earth's core would stop producing a magnetic field
questions.explanation: Without an atmosphere there is no greenhouse effect: heat radiated by the Earth would escape to space, the planet would be too cold, and liquid water and breathable oxygen would be lost.

questions.question: Mercury has an atmosphere about 100 times thinner than Earth's.
questions.explanation: It is Mars whose atmosphere is 100 times thinner than Earth's; Mercury has no atmosphere at all.

questions.question: A freely suspended magnet always settles in a fixed direction because:
options: The Sun pulls the magnet toward itself
Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet
Air currents push the magnet steadily
The magnet is attracted by the Moon
questions.explanation: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, so a freely suspended magnet aligns with the Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: What is believed to be the origin of the Earth's magnetic field?
options: Spinning of the crust around the mantle
Flow of ocean water across the globe
Movement of molten iron in the core
Solar wind striking the atmosphere
questions.explanation: It is believed that the movement of molten iron in Earth's core may be the origin of its magnetic field.

questions.question: High-energy particles that come from far across the universe are called:
options: Solar winds
Radio waves
Ozone gases
Cosmic rays
questions.explanation: Particles from far across the universe are cosmic rays; those coming from the Sun are the solar wind.

questions.question: High-energy particles that come from the Sun are called the:
options: Solar wind
Cosmic rays
Ozone layer
Moonlight
questions.explanation: The stream of particles from the Sun is called the solar wind; cosmic rays come from far across the universe.

questions.question: Select the TWO harmful effects that space particles could have, according to the chapter.
options: Damage the atmosphere
Reduce the ozone layer
Increase Earth's gravity
Cool down the Earth's core
questions.explanation: Cosmic rays and the solar wind can damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer, letting in more harmful UV rays. They do not affect gravity or the core.

questions.question: If space particles reduced the ozone layer, what would be the direct consequence for life?
options: Less sunlight reaches the surface
More harmful UV rays reach Earth
Earth's gravity becomes weaker
Oceans would start to evaporate
questions.explanation: A thinner ozone layer lets in more harmful ultraviolet rays, which can damage living cells and affect life on Earth.

questions.question: Imagine the Earth's magnetic field suddenly disappeared. What problem would arise?
options: The Earth would gradually drift out of its orbit around the Sun
All compasses would point towards the Sun instead of north
More harmful particles would damage the atmosphere and ozone
The atmosphere would become much thicker and far warmer
questions.explanation: The magnetic field pushes cosmic rays and solar wind away. Without it, these particles would damage the atmosphere, thin the ozone layer and let in more UV — harming life. Orbits depend on gravity, not magnetism.

questions.question: The Earth's magnetic field pushes many harmful space particles away, keeping the atmosphere safe.
questions.explanation: The magnetic field acts like a protective shield, deflecting many high-energy particles and so protecting the atmosphere and life.

questions.question: Cosmic rays are high-energy particles that come from the Sun.
questions.explanation: Particles from the Sun are called the solar wind. Cosmic rays come from far across the universe.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed by the chapter as a factor that helps make Earth a planet where life can thrive?
options: Its position in the solar system
Its size and atmosphere
Its magnetic field
Its many volcanoes
questions.explanation: The chapter sums up the factors as Earth's position (allowing liquid water), its size, its atmosphere and its magnetic field. Volcanoes are not mentioned.

questions.question: Select the TWO protective 'shields' the chapter describes.
options: Ozone layer blocking ultraviolet rays
Magnetic field deflecting charged particles
Crust blocking cosmic rays
Hydrosphere absorbing the solar wind
questions.explanation: The ozone layer shields life from UV rays, and the magnetic field shields the atmosphere from high-energy particles. The crust and hydrosphere are not described as shields.

questions.question: In photosynthesis, plants take in which materials to make food?
options: Carbon dioxide from air and water from soil
Oxygen from air and minerals from rocks
Nitrogen from air and water from rain
Carbon dioxide from soil and water from air
questions.explanation: In the presence of sunlight, plants take carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil to prepare food, releasing oxygen.

questions.question: Which gas released during photosynthesis is needed by living things for respiration?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Methane
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases oxygen, which humans, animals and plants use for respiration.

questions.question: About what fraction of the Earth's surface is covered with water?
options: About 50 per cent
About 30 per cent
About 70 per cent
About 90 per cent
questions.explanation: Water covers about 70 per cent of the Earth's surface — in ponds, lakes, rivers, springs, seas, oceans and groundwater.

questions.question: What does the term 'hydrosphere' refer to?
options: All the air around Earth
All living things on Earth
All rocks and soil on Earth
All the water on Earth
questions.explanation: All the water on Earth — in oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater and so on — forms the hydrosphere.

questions.question: Because water is a good solvent, what role does it play in plants?
options: transports nutrients from soil to leaves
blocks UV rays from reaching leaves
produces oxygen inside the leaves
holds the plant upright in the wind
questions.explanation: Water dissolves nutrients and carries them from the soil to the leaves of plants.

questions.question: Select the TWO roles of water in animals that the chapter mentions.
options: Regulates body temperature
Aids digestion
Produces genetic material
Blocks cosmic rays
questions.explanation: In animals, water regulates body temperature, aids digestion and ensures hydration — all essential for health and life.

questions.question: Water vapour forms clouds that bring rain or snow. What does this rain or snow do?
options: Forms the ozone layer in the atmosphere
Refills rivers, lakes and underground water
Breaks rocks down into soil minerals
Carries pollen from flower to flower
questions.explanation: Rain and snow refill rivers, lakes and underground water, keeping the hydrosphere going.

questions.question: Which statement about the hydrosphere is NOT correct?
options: It is home to organisms from planktons to whales
Freshwater from it is needed to grow crops worldwide
Scientists have fully explored life in the deep oceans
It includes groundwater as well as the oceans and seas
questions.explanation: The chapter says we still know little about what lives deep in the oceans — many life forms are still being discovered.

questions.question: Rainfall affects the kinds of plants and animals that can live in a place.
questions.explanation: The chapter says rainfall affects which plants and animals can live in a place, and moving air shapes weather and rainfall.

questions.question: The greenhouse effect on Earth is so strong that most of Earth's water exists as vapour.
questions.explanation: Earth's greenhouse effect is MILD — just enough to keep the temperature high enough for water to remain liquid, not to turn it into vapour.

questions.question: The chapter calls Earth's greenhouse effect 'mild'. Why is even this mild effect important?
options: It makes Earth the hottest planet in the solar system
It stops all heat from ever leaving the Earth
It blocks ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
It keeps temperature just high enough for liquid water
questions.explanation: The mild greenhouse effect keeps the temperature just high enough for water to remain liquid; without it Earth would lose heat to space and freeze.

questions.question: According to the chapter, moving air shapes:
options: weather and rainfall
the ozone shield
the magnetic field
the Earth's orbit
questions.explanation: Moving air shapes weather and rainfall, which in turn influence farming, water supply and life on land.

questions.question: What is the geosphere?
options: Liquid parts: oceans, rivers, lakes
Solid parts: rocks, soils, minerals
Gas layer: air around the Earth
Living parts: plants, animals, microbes
questions.explanation: The solid parts of the Earth — rocks, soils and minerals — are known as the geosphere.

questions.question: Which nutrients does the chapter name as being present in soil for plants to grow?
options: Oxygen and hydrogen
Carbon and chlorine
Nitrogen and potassium
Calcium and sodium
questions.explanation: Soil is rich in nutrients like nitrogen and potassium that plants need to grow.

questions.question: Where do the nutrients in soil come from?
options: Rainwater carrying salts up from the oceans
Carbon dioxide absorbed from the atmosphere
Sunlight absorbed by the surface of the soil
Slow breakdown of rocks and remains of living things
questions.explanation: Soil nutrients come from the slow breakdown of rocks and the remains of plants and animals.

questions.question: Select the TWO things the chapter says minerals of the crust give us.
options: Salt
Coal
Timber
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Minerals give us salt, coal, oil and metals like iron and copper. Timber comes from trees and oxygen from the atmosphere.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of geodiversity?
options: Different landforms like mountains, valleys, and deserts
Variety of bird calls heard chirping in a forest
Changing weather patterns during the monsoon months
Number of different types of fish living in a pond
questions.explanation: Geodiversity is the variety of landforms, rocks, soils and the processes that shape them. Variety of birds or fish is biodiversity; weather is not geodiversity.

questions.question: What does the biosphere include?
options: Only the plants and animals living on land
All living beings and the places they live
Only the water bodies and their creatures
All the non-living rocks and minerals
questions.explanation: The biosphere is all living beings together with the places where they live — land, water and air.

questions.question: What role do decomposers play in nature's system?
options: Make food using sunlight and carbon dioxide
Eat plants and pass the energy on to predators
Break down dead matter and return nutrients to soil
Trap heat in the atmosphere like CO2 does
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, completing the cycle between plants, animals and soil.

questions.question: Cutting down a forest can affect several things, according to the chapter. Which is NOT among them?
options: The rainfall that the region receives
The soil and the quality of the air
The animals living in that place
The Earth's magnetic field strength
questions.explanation: The chapter lists rainfall, soil, air quality and the animals living there. The magnetic field comes from molten iron in the core and is unaffected by forests.

questions.question: Geodiversity helps create unique habitats where different types of life can thrive.
questions.explanation: The variety of landforms, rocks and soils, and the processes that shape them, create unique habitats for life.

questions.question: Soil, rocks and water are only a lifeless background and do not shape how life develops.
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that non-living parts like soil, rocks and water 'aren't just a background' — they help shape the story of life itself.

questions.question: The chapter says Earth is like a 'giant teamwork project'. What keeps the planet habitable?
options: Everything working together in balance
The Sun's energy acting entirely alone
The oxygen in the atmosphere by itself
Humans carefully managing all of nature
questions.explanation: Life survives not because of one thing but because land, air, water and living things support and affect one another in balance.

questions.question: A city cuts down a large patch of forest for roads and buildings. Which effect is most likely, based on the chapter?
options: A noticeably stronger magnetic field over the city
Changed rainfall and loss of local plants and animals
A much thicker ozone layer forming above the city
A cooler local climate because trees no longer block wind
questions.explanation: Even a small change like cutting a forest can impact rainfall, soil, air quality and the animals that live there. Forests do not affect the magnetic field or ozone layer.

questions.question: Which process ensures the continuity of life on Earth?
options: Respiration
Photosynthesis
Reproduction
Pollination
questions.explanation: If plants and animals did not reproduce, life would eventually disappear. Reproduction ensures each type of organism continues to exist.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what are genes?
options: Nutrients stored inside the soil
Gases stored in the atmosphere
Minerals stored in the Earth's crust
Instructions stored inside every cell
questions.explanation: Genes (genetic material) are instructions stored inside every cell — like a detailed instruction manual for making blood, bones, muscles or skin.

questions.question: What does the example of camels developing humps to store fat illustrate?
options: Changes passed on can help survival in new environments
Offspring are always exact copies of their parents
Animals choose the features they want to develop
Deserts cause genes to disappear from cells
questions.explanation: Reproduction allows small changes in the instructions passed down; over time such changes — like humps storing fat — can help survival in a new environment.

questions.question: Some bacteria have become resistant to antibiotics. What does the chapter use this to show?
options: Antibiotics make bacteria reproduce asexually
Even microbes evolve through small changes passed on
Bacteria copy instructions from human cells to survive
Microbes cannot change over generations
questions.explanation: The chapter says even microbes evolve — antibiotic resistance helps bacteria persist, an example of changes helping survival.

questions.question: Which statement about reproduction is NOT correct?
options: It keeps each kind of organism continuing
It allows small changes to pass to offspring
It only ever produces exact copies of the parent
Over generations it can lead to new life forms
questions.explanation: Reproduction does more than copy — it also allows small changes to pass down, which can add up to new features and even new types of living beings. Only ASEXUAL reproduction gives exact copies.

questions.question: In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces new individuals that are exact copies of itself.
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves one parent whose offspring are exact copies in terms of the instructions inside the cell.

questions.question: In sexual reproduction, each offspring is an exact copy of one of its two parents.
questions.explanation: Instructions from two parents combine, so offspring share traits with both parents but are not exactly like either.

questions.question: Why does a calf always grow into a cow, and a kitten into a cat?
options: The mother feeds the calf only on cow's milk for years
The calf grows up in the same field as its mother did
The calf carefully copies the behaviour of adult cows
Parents pass instructions on how to develop from a single cell
questions.explanation: Parents pass genetic instructions to their offspring on how to develop from a single cell, ensuring the young resemble them.

questions.question: How can reproduction lead to BOTH similarity (a cow gives birth to a cow) AND variation (differences in colour or height)?
options: Sexual reproduction mixes instructions from two parents
Asexual reproduction mixes instructions from two parents
Variation comes only from the food offspring eat
Similarity comes from parents teaching their young
questions.explanation: In sexual reproduction instructions from two parents combine — keeping useful features (similarity) while allowing new ones to appear (variation).

questions.question: Which TWO examples does the chapter give of changes that helped living things survive?
options: Camels developing humps to store fat
Bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics
Cats growing wings to escape dogs
Cows learning to lay eggs
questions.explanation: The chapter cites camels' humps (fat storage for deserts) and antibiotic-resistant bacteria as changes that helped survival.

questions.question: Inside a cell, what guides the formation of bones, muscles or skin?
options: Different foods eaten by the parent
Different instructions within the genes
Different temperatures of the body
Different minerals in drinking water
questions.explanation: Genes contain different instructions — some tell the cell how to make blood, others guide the formation of bones, muscles or skin.

questions.question: Over many generations, small differences arising from sexual reproduction can add up to big differences and even new life forms.
questions.explanation: The mixing of instructions keeps useful features while allowing new ones; over many generations these small differences can lead to new life forms.

questions.question: What is vegetative propagation?
options: Growing a new plant from a seed in the soil
Joining pollen and ovule to form a zygote
Growing a new plant from a leaf, stem or root
Spreading seeds through birds and animals
questions.explanation: Many plants reproduce when a part — leaf, stem or root — is planted in soil. This is vegetative propagation, a form of asexual reproduction.

questions.question: Select the TWO plant parts used in Activity 13.3 to grow new plants.
options: Stem cutting of a money plant
'Eyes' of a sprouted potato
Seeds of a mango
Flower of a rose
questions.explanation: Activity 13.3 uses a money-plant stem cutting, the 'eyes' of a sprouted potato, or a piece of ginger — all vegetative propagation.

questions.question: Bamboo and sugarcane grow into new plants although their seeds are rarely seen. How?
options: They produce seeds only underground
They are pollinated by wind at night
They grow from gametes in the soil
They reproduce by vegetative propagation
questions.explanation: Plants like bamboo and sugarcane grow from parts of the plant (stem pieces) — vegetative propagation — so seeds are not needed.

questions.question: How do single-celled organisms like bacteria and amoeba reproduce?
options: Dividing into two identical individuals
Growing buds that break off the body
Regrowing from small cut fragments
Joining male and female gametes
questions.explanation: Bacteria and amoeba divide into two identical individuals — asexual reproduction in single-celled organisms.

questions.question: How does Hydra, a simple animal, reproduce asexually?
options: Dividing into two equal halves
Growing tiny buds that break off
Regrowing from a cut fragment
Laying fertilised eggs in water
questions.explanation: Hydra grows tiny buds on its body that break off and grow into new individuals.

questions.question: Scientists study Planaria to understand which process?
options: Photosynthesis in animals
Pollination in flowers
Regeneration in animals
Antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: Planaria, a flatworm, can regrow from a fragment of its body, so scientists study it to understand regeneration.

questions.question: Which organism is matched CORRECTLY with its asexual method?
options: Hydra — divide into two identical cells
Amoeba — grow buds on the body
Planaria — produce pollen grains
Algae — regrow from small cut parts
questions.explanation: Algae can regrow from small cut parts. Hydra buds, amoeba divides into two, and Planaria regrows from a fragment — pollen belongs to flowering plants.

questions.question: Only plants can reproduce asexually; all animals need two parents.
questions.explanation: Microbes (bacteria, amoeba) and simple animals like Hydra and Planaria also reproduce asexually.

questions.question: In Activity 13.3, what are you asked to record each day?
options: Days taken for roots, stem and leaves to appear
Change in colour of the soil each morning
Number of insects visiting the growing plant
Amount of water evaporating from the glass
questions.explanation: You watch the planted parts daily and note how many days it takes for roots, stem and leaves to appear, and when the first new leaf comes.

questions.question: Activity 13.3 suggests putting the money-plant cutting in a glass container. Why?
options: Glass supplies the nutrients the plant needs
It makes root growth easy to observe
Glass blocks sunlight so roots grow faster
Water in glass stays warmer than soil
questions.explanation: A transparent glass container lets you observe the roots as they appear — the activity is about observing growth.

questions.question: A piece of ginger planted in soil grows into a new plant. Which type of reproduction is this?
options: Sexual, by pollination and fertilisation
Asexual, by budding like hydra
Asexual, by vegetative propagation
Sexual, by joining two mating types
questions.explanation: A new plant growing from a stem piece (ginger) is vegetative propagation — asexual, with a single parent.

questions.question: Select the TWO plants the chapter names as growing by vegetative propagation.
options: Ginger
Bamboo
Banyan (from a bird-dropped seed)
Mango grown from a seed
questions.explanation: Ginger, potato, money plant, bamboo and sugarcane are the chapter's vegetative propagation examples. The banyan in the wall crack grew from a seed — sexual reproduction.

questions.question: How much of a parent's genetic material does a gamete carry?
options: All of the parent's genetic material
Twice the parent's genetic material
None of the parent's genetic material
Half of the parent's genetic material
questions.explanation: Gametes are specialised reproductive cells carrying only half the parent's genetic material; two gametes join to give a complete set.

questions.question: Why doesn't the amount of genetic instructions double in every generation of sexual reproduction?
options: Each gamete carries only half, so joining makes a full set
Offspring throw away the extra copies soon after birth
Only one of the two parents passes on its instructions
Cells shrink the instructions as the baby grows bigger
questions.explanation: Each parent's gamete carries half of its genetic material; when male and female gametes join, the new cell has one complete set — half from each parent.

questions.question: Where are pollen grains, the male gametes of a flowering plant, found?
options: The ovule
The anther
The fruit
The stem
questions.explanation: Pollen grains are found inside the anther of a flower; ovules, the female gametes, are deep inside the flower.

questions.question: Which are the female gametes of a flowering plant?
options: Pollen grains inside the anther
Petals around the flower
Ovules deep inside the flower
Seeds inside the fruit
questions.explanation: Ovules, found deep inside the flower, are the female gametes; pollen grains are the male gametes.

questions.question: What is pollination?
options: Joining of male and female gametes
Forming a seed from a zygote
Spreading seeds by birds
Carrying pollen to another flower
questions.explanation: Pollination is the carrying of pollen to another flower by wind, insects or animals. The joining of gametes is fertilisation.

questions.question: After fertilisation in a flower, what develops into the fruit?
options: The fleshy part of the flower around the ovule
The zygote that forms right after fertilisation
The anther after it has released its pollen
The pollen grain after it lands on a flower
questions.explanation: The zygote becomes the seed, while the fleshy part of the flower around the ovule develops into the fruit.

questions.question: How might a banyan seedling come to sprout in a crack in a wall?
options: Wind carried the pollen grain into the crack
A bird ate the fruit and excreted the seed there
The wall absorbed nutrients from the rain
A root of a nearby banyan grew into the wall
questions.explanation: Birds and animals eat fruit and drop seeds far from the parent plant; a banyan seed excreted by a bird can sprout in a wall crack after rain.

questions.question: Tiny plants appear in cracks on a school wall after the monsoon. What helped them grow there?
options: Strong sunlight baking the seeds in the wall
Cement dust supplying nitrogen to the seeds
Rainwater, allowing seeds to use stored nutrients
Cold weather freezing the seeds beforehand
questions.explanation: When seeds get water, they use their stored nutrients to grow roots and shoots. The monsoon rains supplied the water the seeds needed.

questions.question: Select the TWO pollen carriers the chapter mentions.
options: Wind
Insects
Rivers
Sunlight
questions.explanation: Pollen is carried to another flower by wind, insects or animals.

questions.question: Flowering plants have male and female parts.
questions.explanation: Even flowering plants have male parts (anther with pollen) and female parts (ovules).

questions.question: Pollen grains are the female gametes of a flowering plant.
questions.explanation: Pollen grains in the anther are the MALE gametes; ovules are the female gametes.

questions.question: In sexual reproduction, why are offspring different from their parents?
options: They grow up in quite different climates and places
They eat quite different kinds of food while growing
They acquire brand-new instructions after their birth
They get mixed instructions (genes) from both parents
questions.explanation: Each gamete carries a different set of instructions, and these mix in a new way each time — so each child is unique, sharing traits with both parents.

questions.question: Some bacteria and yeast have two 'mating types'. What do these act like?
options: The two parents in sexual reproduction
The two halves of a dividing amoeba
The buds growing on a hydra's body
The anther and the fruit of a flower
questions.explanation: The two mating types act like the two parents (male and female) in sexual reproduction.

questions.question: When a seed gets water, it uses stored nutrients to grow roots and shoots.
questions.explanation: Seeds use their stored nutrients to grow roots and shoots once they receive water — as seen in germination.

questions.question: What is the male gamete called in animals?
options: Egg
Sperm
Pollen
Ovule
questions.explanation: In animals the gametes are sperm (male) and eggs (female).

questions.question: Where does fertilisation take place in fish and frogs?
options: Inside the female's body
Inside the egg after laying
In water, outside the body
In the soil near the pond
questions.explanation: Male and female fish or frogs eject sperm and eggs into the water, where they combine to form the zygote.

questions.question: In birds and mammals, where and how does fertilisation occur?
options: In open water where the eggs and sperm are released
Inside the laid egg during the hatching period
On the ground shortly after the egg has been laid
Inside the female's body when sperm swim to the egg
questions.explanation: Sperm are deposited inside the female's body and fertilisation takes place when the sperm swim towards the egg.

questions.question: In birds, when does the zygote develop into an embryo?
options: After the egg is laid, during hatching
Inside the mother before laying
In water after the eggs are released
Inside the mother until the chick is born
questions.explanation: In birds the fertilised egg is laid, and the zygote develops into an embryo after laying, during the hatching process.

questions.question: Why must a bird put so much 'food' into each egg it lays?
options: The chick eats the shell after hatching
The embryo must be fed until it hatches
The mother needs the food while sitting
The food keeps the egg from freezing
questions.explanation: The food in the egg has to last for the developing embryo until it hatches — one strategy for supplying nutrition to the embryo.

questions.question: In most mammals, who provides the food and oxygen the developing baby needs?
options: The yolk stored inside the egg
The water in which the egg floats
The mother's body, until birth
The father through the gametes
questions.explanation: In most mammals the embryo develops inside the female's body, and the mother's body provides all the food and oxygen until birth.

questions.question: Why don't dogs or cows lay eggs like hens do?
options: They produce no reproductive gametes at all
Their eggs would be far too heavy to be laid
They reproduce asexually by growing buds
Their embryos develop inside the mother's body
questions.explanation: Dogs and cows are mammals: the zygote develops into an embryo inside the mother, who supplies food and oxygen until birth — so no egg is laid.

questions.question: Select the TWO animals whose zygote develops into an embryo in water.
options: Frog
Fish
Sparrow
Cow
questions.explanation: In fish and frogs both fertilisation and development of the zygote into an embryo happen in water. Birds develop in laid eggs; mammals inside the mother.

questions.question: In birds, the zygote develops into an embryo inside the mother's body before the egg is laid.
questions.explanation: In birds the development of the zygote into an embryo happens AFTER the egg is laid, during hatching.

questions.question: Which feature do birds and mammals SHARE in reproduction?
options: Sperm are deposited inside the female's body
The embryo develops outside the mother's body
Eggs and sperm are released into water
The young are born live rather than hatched
questions.explanation: In both birds and mammals sperm are deposited inside the female and fertilisation happens there; after that step the two groups differ.

questions.question: What is a zygote?
options: The specialised cell carrying half the genes
The cell formed when male and female gametes join
The fleshy part that becomes the fruit
The male gamete produced by the anther
questions.explanation: When male and female gametes join they form a zygote — a new cell with a complete set of instructions.

questions.question: Select the TWO ways the chapter describes embryos receiving nutrition.
options: Food stored in the egg (birds)
The mother's body (most mammals)
Nutrients absorbed from pond water
Sunlight passing through the egg shell
questions.explanation: Birds pack food into each egg to last until hatching; in most mammals the mother's body supplies food and oxygen until birth.

questions.question: Which three challenges make up the 'triple planetary crisis'?
options: Earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions
Overpopulation, poverty and widespread disease
Climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution
Deforestation, mining, overfishing
questions.explanation: The biggest environmental challenges — climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution — are together called the triple planetary crisis.

questions.question: Burning fossil fuels releases which greenhouse gases named in the chapter?
options: Oxygen gas and nitrogen gas
Ozone and water vapour
Hydrogen and helium
Carbon dioxide and methane
questions.explanation: Burning coal and oil releases greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane, which trap more heat and cause global warming.

questions.question: Why can't the Earth absorb the extra carbon from burning fossil fuels?
options: It was locked underground for millions of years and is released too fast
Plants have completely stopped photosynthesis in warmer weather
Ocean planktons absorb only oxygen and never carbon dioxide
Methane in the air blocks trees from taking in carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels release extra carbon locked underground for millions of years; the Earth cannot absorb it fast enough, so heat builds up.

questions.question: Which TWO absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, helping Earth keep its carbon balance?
options: Trees and plants
Tiny ocean planktons
Coal deposits underground
Melting ice caps
questions.explanation: Normally trees, plants and even tiny ocean planktons absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, keeping a balance.

questions.question: If a small rise in temperature melts the ice caps, what does the chapter say could follow?
options: Oceans become fresh and fish disappear
Sea levels rise and coastal cities may flood
The ozone layer becomes much thicker
The Earth's orbit changes its shape
questions.explanation: Melting ice caps raise sea levels, which could flood many coastal cities; extreme weather and loss of species may also follow.

questions.question: What does the chapter call 'climate change'?
options: Daily changes in temperature between the day and the night
The regular seasonal change from summer to winter every year
Long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather patterns
Sudden thunderstorms caused by fast-moving masses of air
questions.explanation: Climate change means long-term changes in temperature, rainfall and weather patterns — not daily or seasonal variation.

questions.question: If grasses vanish from a habitat, what chain of effects does the chapter describe?
options: Tigers and foxes thrive because deer are easier to find
Grasshoppers increase since deer no longer compete with them
Soil becomes richer as grass stops using up its nutrients
Deer and grasshoppers struggle, then tigers and foxes lose food
questions.explanation: Herbivores like deer and grasshoppers that feed on grass struggle; without herbivores, predators like tigers and foxes lose their food too.

questions.question: Burning fossil fuels like coal and oil releases greenhouse gases.
questions.explanation: Coal and oil release carbon dioxide and methane when burnt, trapping extra heat in the atmosphere.

questions.question: Even a large rise in global temperature has little effect on sea levels or weather.
questions.explanation: The chapter says even a SMALL increase can melt ice caps, raise sea levels, cause extreme weather and make many species disappear.

questions.question: A friend says, 'The Earth has always had climate changes, so today's warming is nothing new.' Which reply best uses the chapter?
options: Burning fossil fuels now releases locked carbon faster than Earth can absorb
The Earth has never before experienced any kind of climate change
Warming today is caused mainly by the Sun moving closer to Earth
Climate change only affects the ice caps, so it is not really new
questions.explanation: Today's warming is driven by human burning of fossil fuels, releasing carbon locked away for millions of years faster than plants and planktons can absorb it.

questions.question: A village's temperature has been rising and its rainfall has become unpredictable. What is the likely cause?
options: A weakening of the Earth's magnetic field
Climate change driven by increased greenhouse gases
The Earth moving out of the habitable zone
A thickening of the ozone layer over the village
questions.explanation: Long-term changes in temperature and rainfall patterns are climate change, caused by extra greenhouse gases trapping heat.

questions.question: Normally trees, plants and ocean planktons absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, keeping Earth's carbon in balance.
questions.explanation: The chapter says Earth normally keeps a balance because trees, plants and tiny ocean planktons absorb CO2 as they grow.

questions.question: Air pollution from factories, vehicles and burning fuels can lead to:
options: earthquakes and floods
tides and currents
smog and acid rain
ozone and oxygen
questions.explanation: Air pollution can cause breathing problems, damage crops, and lead to smog and acid rain.

questions.question: In which year was the Montreal Protocol agreed?
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol (1987) helped reduce harmful chemicals like CFCs, allowing the ozone layer to slowly recover.

questions.question: What did the Montreal Protocol achieve?
options: Reduced CFCs, helping the ozone layer recover
Reduced carbon dioxide, slowing global warming
Reduced plastic waste in the oceans
Reduced methane from farms and factories
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol reduced chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), letting the ozone layer slowly recover.

questions.question: What did the Earth Summit of 1992 lead to?
options: A worldwide ban on CFCs to protect the ozone layer
International efforts on climate change and biodiversity
A legally binding goal to limit warming to below 1.5 °C
Firm commitments to switch entirely to renewable energy
questions.explanation: The Earth Summit (1992) led to international efforts on climate change and biodiversity. CFCs were the Montreal Protocol; the 1.5 °C goal came with the Paris Agreement.

questions.question: What goal did the Paris Agreement (2015) set?
options: Limit global warming to below 5 °C
Stop all use of fossil fuels by 2025
Limit global warming to below 1.5 °C
Recover the ozone layer by 2050
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement set a goal to limit global warming to below 1.5 °C — but as of 2025 the world is not on track to meet it.

questions.question: The Kyoto Protocol, which committed countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, dates from:
questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol (2005) and the Paris Agreement (2015) committed countries to cut emissions. 1987 is Montreal; 1992 is the Earth Summit.

questions.question: Which statement about global environmental agreements is NOT correct?
options: As of 2025 the world is on track to meet the Paris goal
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 targeted harmful CFCs
Kyoto and Paris committed countries to cut emissions
The Earth Summit took place in the year 1992
questions.explanation: The chapter says that as of 2025 the world is NOT on track to limit warming to below 1.5 °C — much more action is needed.

questions.question: Select the TWO sources of water and soil pollution the chapter names.
options: Factory, farm and plastic waste
Excess fertilisers
Cosmic rays from space
Solar wind from the Sun
questions.explanation: Factory, farm and plastic waste harm aquatic life, while excess fertilisers and poor waste disposal pollute soil.

questions.question: What effects do excess fertilisers and poor waste disposal have on soil?
options: Increase crop yield while cleaning the surrounding groundwater
Reduce crop yield and spread harmful substances through the food chain
Thicken the ozone layer and greatly reduce ultraviolet radiation
Strengthen the soil so that plants need much less water to grow
questions.explanation: Excess fertilisers and poor waste disposal pollute soil, reduce crop yield and spread harmful substances through the food chain.

questions.question: Which pair are examples of renewable energy given in the chapter?
options: Coal and oil
Petrol and gas
Solar and wind
Wood and charcoal
questions.explanation: Protecting the climate means using renewable energy like solar and wind instead of fossil fuels.

questions.question: Because the Earth's systems are separate, damage to the hydrosphere does not affect the biosphere.
questions.explanation: The hydrosphere, biosphere, atmosphere and geosphere are all connected — damage to one can affect the others.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say preserving biodiversity is key?
options: More species means more carbon dioxide released
It thickens the ozone layer over forests
It increases the Earth's magnetic field
Diverse ecosystems are stronger and more balanced
questions.explanation: Diverse ecosystems are stronger and more balanced, so preserving biodiversity helps sustain life.

questions.question: Which small changes does the chapter say could endanger life on Earth?
options: Slightly less oxygen or ozone, or a slightly higher temperature
A slightly stronger magnetic field or a bit more yearly rainfall
A few more volcanic eruptions or earthquakes occurring each year
A very slight change in the length of a day or a year
questions.explanation: A little less or more oxygen, a little lower or higher temperature, or a little less ozone could endanger life — the balance is delicate.

questions.question: Select the TWO actions the chapter lists for protecting the climate.
options: Using renewable energy like solar and wind
Choosing environmentally friendly ways to travel
Burning more coal for cheaper electricity
Clearing forests to build solar farms
questions.explanation: Protecting the climate means cutting greenhouse gases: renewable energy, improving energy use, and environmentally friendly travel.

questions.question: Reusing, repairing and recycling items like clothes and plastic reduce pollution and waste.
questions.explanation: The chapter says everyone can help — reusing, repairing and recycling reduce pollution and waste, and small actions add up.
